newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: French defence minister lobbies in UAE for planes.
newsitem.headline: French defence minister lobbies in UAE for planes.

text.p: French Defence Minister Charles Millon, eager for a long-awaited $6 billion order for up to 80 warplanes, left Abu Dhabi on Sunday after last-minute lobbying ahead of an upcoming arms show, industry sources said.

He arrived in the United Arab Emirates capital on Saturday night and held talks with President Sheikh Zaid bin Sultan al-Nahayan and the country's top military procurement officer before departing for Malaysia, the French embassy said.

The embassy refused to comment on the purpose of Millon's visit and would not say whether he had originally planned the stop in Abu Dhabi -- a week before he is due here to attend the IDEX arms show that begins next Sunday.

But defence industry executives said Millon was making one final sales drive before the show, when the UAE is expected to announce several arms deals at an event expected to draw 700 companies from 45 countries.
"You can bet Millon's letter to Sheikh Zaid from the French president concerned the warplane package," said one.
"The UAE probably had more questions on the French offer and he has made some adjustments like prices. Things are heating up before IDEX."
Market rumours have been rife for months that Abu Dhabi would award the aircraft contract to the remaining bidders -- France's Dassault Aviation and American firm Lockheed Martin Corp -- at IDEX.
The package, potentially worth $6 billion, could be the world's last contract of its size this century.
"The airplane deal is in the air," said another industry executive. "We were surprised that Millon came. The big deals are often cracked at IDEX."
It was not possible to confirm rumours in a market that has kept arms manufacturers guessing for years.
But the possibility of clinching a lucrative contract has shifted the French and American lobbying machines into top gear.
The United States, which has also sent many officials here, has been banking on cashing in political credit earned in the Gulf War to steer most or all of the package to Lockheed Martin.
Paris, meanwhile, has enjoyed a lucrative history in Abu Dhabi, its partner in a defence pact.

France has already supplied the UAE with Mirage planes and AMX tanks. The UAE ordered French Leclerc battle tanks for $3.62 billion in 1993, in preference to British and American rivals, and awarded a $235 million deal to the Franco-German Eurocopter company in 1995 for new helicopters and upgrades.

Dassault has long boasted that France's value as an alternative arms source lies in its willingness to sell state-of-the-art weapons because the United States is selective about arms export approvals.
Market players say it is always hard to predict whether and when years of intensive lobbying will pay off.

"Millon is trying to stress military cooperation. This could be France's last drive before a final decision is made. But it could happen at IDEX, or by the end of year. Who knows?" said a military attache.
